kiš: Kish — city of the first dynasty after the Flood, to which the list returns after the Flood; written with the KIŠ sign plus the place-determinative KI (unread), as kiš{ki}; it has no case ending on the prism, 'in' being understood
ĝa₂-ur: Ĝa-ur (Langdon Gà-ur) — first king of Kish after the Flood; GA₂ (Langdon's 'MAL') + UR; how the name was really pronounced is uncertain
gul-la-{d}nidaba-an-na-[…]-el: Gulla-Nidaba-anna… — king of Kish, the second named in the dynasty; GUL-LA, divine determinative, the Nidaba (Nisaba, grain-goddess) sign NAGA, AN-NA, a broken stretch left unread, then EL; Langdon notes Gulla-ezen-an-na… as another possible reading, so the fourth sign is uncertain
[…]: a lost stretch of text — a gap in the prism where the signs are broken away (the four lost lines at the top of Col. II, which Langdon judges held two royal names with their reigns)
ba-[…]: a royal name beginning Ba-, the rest lost; only the BA sign survives (Langdon restores Ba[ba?-gul-?e?] with his own question marks, too uncertain to show)
bu-[…]: a royal name beginning Bu-, followed by the divine determinative, so a god's name; the rest lost (Langdon restores 'Bu-Sin (?)' after a Nippur fragment, with question marks)
ga-li₂-bu-um: Galibum — king of Kish; li₂ is the NI sign (Langdon lí); the name looks Semitic (Akkadian-type -um ending); Langdon notes the same king on three Nippur duplicates
ka-lu-mu: Kalumu — king of Kish; Langdon reads Ka-lu-mu-mu, but his own copy shows only two MU signs, so the second MU is taken as 'years' and a final -um may simply be unwritten; Nippur copies (Ga-lu-mu-um, Ka-lu-mu-um) support Kalumum
dug₄-ga-gi₄-ib: Duggagib (Langdon Dúg-ga-gí-ib) — king of Kish; first sign KA, readable dug₄ 'speak' or zu₂ 'tooth'; Langdon reads dug₄ and rejects Poebel's zu-ga-gi-ib, so the name's reading is uncertain
a₂-tab: Atab — king of Kish; a₂ is the A₂ sign ('arm'), tab the TAB sign ('double'); as a name its meaning is not clear
a₂-tab-ba: Atabba — king of Kish, following Atab; the added -ba makes a distinct name
ar-pi-u₂-um: Arpium — king of Kish, the first given a father ('son of maš-da'); u₂ is Langdon's ú; second sign (Langdon dā) is shown as DA after his reading but its identification is uncertain; Nippur copies vary the name (Ar-pi-i, Ar-pu-um, Ar-pi-ú)
dumu: son, child — written with the TUR sign, read dumu; in 'dumu X' the son of X; Langdon reads it as 'son'
maš-da: maš-da — Langdon 'a poor man' (written BAR-DA, the sign BAR rather than the usual MAŠ); the sense in the list is uncertain, and 'poor man' is Langdon's, marked (?); his dā sign is drawn like NI, so its identification is uncertain
-ke₄: genitive -ak 'of' + ergative -e, written with the KID sign (Langdon -ge) — marks 'son of X' as the subject of the reign verb; the scribe does not always write it (absent after dumu enmenunna in one line)
e-ta-na: Etana — king of Kish, 'the shepherd who went up to heaven, who made all the foreign lands firm'; reigned 1,500 years; the ascent is the subject of a well-known Babylonian legend; father of Balih
sipa: shepherd — written PA + LU (Langdon sib); a royal title in Etana's entry
lu₂: man; 'the one who …' — introduces a relative ('who') clause; Langdon galu
ba-: ba- — verbal prefix (often of motion away, or a middle/passive sense); in ba-e₃-de₃ 'went up' (with e₃ written UD.DU, final de₃ = NE); the Nippur copies write ba-e₃-da
kur-kur: the foreign lands, all the mountain lands — kur 'mountain, foreign land' doubled as a plural; Langdon renders 'foreign lands'
mu-un-: mu-n- — verbal prefix chain: mu- + -n- 'he' (the doer); in mu-un-gi-na 'he made firm'
gi-n: to make firm, establish — gi-n 'firm, true' (with the -a of the 'who' clause in mu-un-gi-na); Langdon translates 'made the foreign lands faithful'
ba-li-iḫ: Balih — king of Kish, son of Etana; iḫ is the AḪ sign; a Nippur copy spells the name Wa-li-iḫ and gives 410 years
en-me-nun-na: Enmenunna — king of Kish; en 'lord' + me + nun 'prince' + -na, a name of the same shape as the En-men-… kings before the Flood; father of Melam-Kish and Barsalnunna
me-lam-kiš: Melam-Kish — king of Kish, son of Enmenunna; me-lam 'awe-inspiring radiance' + the city name Kish (with its determinative); King's Chronicles read A-lam-kiš-šu, which Langdon calls a scribal error
bar-sal-nun-na: Barsalnunna — king of Kish, a second son of Enmenunna; father of Tupzah; a Nippur copy omits 'son of Enmenunna'
tup-za-aḫ: Tupzah (Langdon Tup-za-aḫ) — king of Kish, son of Barsalnunna; first sign is Langdon's KIŠIB ('not MES'), in Unicode the MES character; its value in the name is uncertain, so the name's real form is too
ti-iz-kar₃: Tizkar (Langdon Ti-iz-kàr) — king of Kish, son of Tupzah; iz is GIŠ; the third sign is read GAN after Langdon's value, but its identification on the copy is uncertain
šu-ši: šu-ši — 'sixty', spelled out as a word (Akkadian šūši) rather than with geš signs; 5 šu-ši + 6 = 306, an unusual way of writing a number
6: six — here the units of 'five sixties and six' (5 šu-ši + 6 = 306)
il-ku-u₃: Ilku (Langdon Il-ku-u, 'Ilkû') — king of Kish; third sign taken as U₃ (ù) though on his copy it is larger than the single corner-wedge U, so uncertain; a Nippur copy may have Il-ku-u-um
il-ta-sa-du-um: Iltasadum — king of Kish; another Semitic-looking name in -um
en-me-en-bara₂-gi-gur: Enmenbaragigur (Langdon En-me-en-bara-gi-gur) — king of Kish, 'the man who made the weapons of the land of Elam bow down'; better known today as Enmebaragesi, the last signs being read differently; father of Agga
ma-da: land, country — in ma-da elam{ki}-ma 'the land of Elam'
elam: Elam — land east of Babylonia; written with the NIM sign plus place-determinative ki, as elam{ki}
-ma: genitive -a(k) 'of', written -ma after m (here elam{ki}-ma 'of Elam')
{ĝeš}: wood determinative (ĝeš, the GIŠ sign) — unread, marks a wooden object; Langdon writes it as a raised ᵍⁱˢ
tukul: weapon, mace — the KU sign with the wood determinative ĝeš (Langdon ᵍⁱˢku); no case ending in the list, 'with weapons' being understood in the closing refrain
ib-ta-an-: ib-ta-n- — verbal prefix chain with -ta- ('from / with'; Langdon takes it as an instrumental infix) and -n- 'he'; the grammar of the line is debated
gam: to bend, bow down; to subdue — with ib-ta-n- 'made bow down'; Langdon translates 'with his weapon subdued'
ag-ga: Agga (Langdon Ag-ga, also cited as Aka) — last king of the first dynasty of Kish, son of Enmenbaragigur; AK + GA; the Agga of the Sumerian story of his conflict with Gilgamesh of Uruk
23: twenty-three — the number of kings in the dynasty's total
iti: month (Langdon ita) — in the dynasty's total of years, months and days
u₄-maš: half a day — u₄ 'day' + maš 'half', maš written with BAR as in maš-da
ba-an-: ba-n- — verbal prefix chain; ba- often gives a passive sense while -n- would ordinarily mark a 'he' who acts, so the passive English of the refrain follows the sense rather than every element
sig₃: to strike, smite — written as one compact sign taken as PA.GAN₂ (Langdon sīg, also printed sig); the identification of the drawn form is uncertain
e₂-an-na: Eanna, 'House of Heaven' — Inanna's temple at Uruk (Langdon É-an-na), standing for the city whose kings come next; e₂ 'house' + an-na 'of heaven'
